title: Disparate Impact Metrics: Scaling Challenges from Theory to Global Deployment
text:
In academic settings, Disparate Impact (DI) serves as a foundational quantitative check, measuring the ratio of selection rates between protected and non-protected groups. Its simplicity allows for straightforward theoretical identification of disparity using static datasets. However, moving this concept to global or large-scale industrial application reveals fundamental hurdles regarding assumption maintenance.

The basic statistical robustness of DI degrades significantly when encountering dynamic data characteristics inherent in real-world systems, such as concept drift, non-stationary distributions, and cascading feature dependencies. Unlike academic tests applied to clean cohorts, industrial datasets are continuous streams where the definition of 'protected group' can shift based on jurisdiction or evolving usage patterns, complicating uniform metric application. Furthermore, treating DI solely as a post-hoc detection tool fails to address the operational complexity that arises when attempts are made to enforce parity across disparate risk categories and decision boundaries in production models.
